newsitem.title: UK: Protestant hold on Belfast under threat in poll.
newsitem.headline: Protestant hold on Belfast under threat in poll.

text.p: Protestant Unionists seemed set to lose political control of Belfast, the heart of British rule in Northern Ireland, as results of municipal elections on Thursday showed gains by Sinn Fein, the political arm of the IRA.

The prospect that Belfast might get its first Irish nationalist mayor was raised after BBC radio's political analysis unit predicted that Unionists would lose power to Sinn Fein and the Catholic-based Social Democratic and Labour (SDLP).

Voters were choosing councillors and majors in 26 districts. Final results were not due until Friday afternoon but the BBC said nationalist parties might also gain overall control of Fermanagh near the the border with the Irish Republic.

Political analysts predicted Sinn Fein's vote would rise some four points from the last municipal election in 1993, matching the 16 per cent support it won in the May 1 parliamentary election, its best performance in 40 years.

Eamon Phoenix, a historian in Irish nationalist politics, said it would be "a major psychological bodyblow" and a stark reversal of history if Unionists, who insist that the province must remain British, lost control of Belfast.
"It looks almost certain that there will be a 26 to 25 result in the City Hall. The 26 would seem to be made up of Sinn Fein, the SDLP and the middle-of-the-road Alliance Party," he told Reuters.
"It is a complete reversal of the municipal history since 1610, when Belfast was officially given town status by the British Crown."

But a leader of the biggest Protestant party, the Ulster Unionists, raised the possibility of a legal challenge to the results, blaming Britain's Northern Ireland Office for handing Sinn Fein a polling day propaganda coup on Wednesday.

Ken Maginnis said a high-profile meeting between officials and a Sinn Fein delegation -- the first since the collapse of an Irish Republican Army truce 16 months ago -- reaped media publicity that could have contravened electoral laws.
"Unfortunately the whole integrity of the process was infringed yesterday by the activities of the Northern Ireland Office," Maginnis told BBC.

"Totally insensitive, they gave Sinn Fein the sort of publicity that a quarter of a million pounds wouldn't have paid for. I believe...There may be grounds for asking that the whole process be declared null and void."

The IRA, which fought a 25-year guerrilla war against British rule, has rejected calls for a second ceasefire. Britain and Ireland insist the violence must end before Sinn Fein can be invited to all-party peace talks.
Wednesday's talks were held after new British Prime Minister Tony Blair eased a ban on contact with Sinn Fein at official level to try to inject new life into a stalled peace process.
